a: Abijah
p: Kings calls this king Abijam. Chronicles calls him Abijah, "my father is the LORD."
b: Chronicles uses Aviyyah (also Aviyyahu, 13:20–21), a name built on the LORD's name. Kings uses Aviyyam (1 Kings 15:1–8). Some scholars think Kings has a copying slip, since final m and h were easy to confuse in some scripts. Others think "Abijam" was a real form of the name, perhaps "father of the sea," and Kings kept it. A few suggest that Kings avoided a name honoring the LORD for a king it judged harshly, while Chronicles, which gives him a heroic speech, uses the pious form. This site keeps each book's own form of a king's name and notes the difference rather than making the names match.

a: His mother's name was Micaiah, Uriel's daughter, from Gibeah.
p: Kings and 11:20 call Abijah's mother Maacah, Absalom's daughter. Here she is Micaiah, Uriel's daughter.
b: Three statements need fitting together. 1 Kings 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 11:20–22 say Abijah's mother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom (Absalom). This verse calls her Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. And 15:16 (like 1 Kings 15:10) calls Maacah the "mother" of Asa, Abijah's son. The Greek here reads "Maacah," so "Micaiah" may be a copying slip in the Hebrew (see the variant). Many readers since Josephus have taken "daughter of Absalom" to mean granddaughter: Uriel married Absalom's daughter Tamar (2 Samuel 14:27), and their daughter Maacah married Rehoboam. "Mother" of Asa would then mean grandmother, or the queen mother who kept her rank. Others think Chronicles here uses a different source than in 11:20.

a: four hundred thousand chosen men
p: Four hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand, with five hundred thousand dead. How should we read such figures?
b: These armies (13:3), Asa's 580,000 and Zerah's "thousand thousands" (14:8–9), and Jehoshaphat's 1,160,000 (17:14–18) are far beyond what Iron Age Judah could field; the whole population was probably well under a quarter of a million. Readers handle this in several ways. Literal: some traditional readers accept the numbers as given. "Thousand" as a unit: the Hebrew elef can mean a clan or military unit, so "400 elef" may once have meant 400 units of a few men each (Mendenhall's proposal for Numbers). Rhetorical: most commentators think the Chronicler used round, swelling numbers on purpose, to show that victory belongs to God, not to the larger army (13:8, 14:11). Copying: numbers were easily changed in transmission. The point in context is the ratio: Judah is outnumbered two to one and still wins.

a: Mount Zemaraim
p: A height on the border between Judah and Israel, near Bethel. Its exact location is unknown.
b: Joshua lists a town Zemaraim in Benjamin, between Beth-arabah and Bethel (Joshua 18:22). The battle is set in the disputed borderland of Benjamin, the same strip that Baasha and Asa fight over later (16:1–6). Abijah speaks from a hilltop, as Jotham did when he shouted his fable to Shechem from Mount Gerizim (Judges 9:7).

a: by a covenant of salt
p: Salt does not rot or spoil. A "covenant of salt" is one meant to last.
b: Salt preserves food, and ancient people sealed agreements by sharing a meal with salt. The phrase appears only three times. Every offering was to be salted with "the salt of your God's covenant" (Leviticus 2:13), and the priests' share is called "a covenant of salt for all time before the LORD" (Numbers 18:19). Abijah applies it to David's line: the kingship is as lasting as the priests' portion. His speech joins the two institutions the north has rejected, David's throne and Aaron's priesthood (13:9–10).

a: Rehoboam was young and timid of heart
p: Rehoboam was forty-one when he became king. Abijah calls him "young" to excuse his father.
b: By 12:13 and 1 Kings 14:21, Rehoboam was forty-one. "Young" (na'ar) here means inexperienced, the word Solomon used of himself (1 Kings 3:7). Kings blames the split on Rehoboam's harsh answer to the people and says it was "from the LORD" (1 Kings 12:13–15; compare 2 Chronicles 10:15). Abijah's speech says nothing of the harsh answer. He blames Jeroboam the rebel slave and the "worthless men" around him. Readers have taken this in two ways: as the Chronicler's own verdict, or as a partisan speech the Chronicler reports in character, which the reader is meant to weigh against chapter 10.

a: the calves of gold that Jeroboam made for you as gods
p: Abijah throws Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan back at the north. It is Chronicles' only mention of them.
b: Jeroboam set up two golden calves and echoed Aaron's words at Sinai: "Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (1 Kings 12:28; compare Exodus 32:4). Chronicles never tells that story, but here Abijah assumes his hearers know it. Whether the calves were meant as idols or as pedestals for the invisible LORD, like the cherubim, is debated (see the golden calf topic); to Abijah they are simply "gods."

a: to be installed
p: The Hebrew idiom "to fill one's hand" means to ordain a priest.
b: Literally, "everyone who comes to fill his hand with a young bull and seven rams." The phrase is the technical term for installing a priest (Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:9, 35; Leviticus 8:33), probably from placing the first portions of the offering in his hands. In Moses' law, the ordination required one bull and two rams (Exodus 29:1). Abijah mocks the northern system: anyone who can afford the animals can buy a priesthood. Kings says the same of Jeroboam: "Anyone who wished, he installed as one of the priests of the high places" (1 Kings 13:33).
orig: לְמַלֵּא יָדוֹ (lemalle yado), "to fill his hand"
r: Exodus 29:1; Exodus 29:9; Exodus 29:35; Leviticus 8:33; 1 Kings 12:31; 1 Kings 13:33

a: no-gods
p: Hebrew "lo elohim," "not gods": a prophetic put-down of idols.
b: The phrase is used by the prophets for idols that have the name of gods without the reality: "a nation that has changed its gods, though they are no-gods" (Jeremiah 2:11; compare Jeremiah 5:7; Jeremiah 16:20; Hosea 8:6). Paul uses the same idea for "so-called gods" (1 Corinthians 8:5; Galatians 4:8).

a: the gold lampstand
p: Solomon made ten golden lampstands. Abijah speaks of one, as in the tabernacle and the Second Temple.
b: Abijah lists the daily round of worship in Jerusalem: morning and evening burnt offerings (Numbers 28:3–8), incense (Exodus 30:7–8), the row of bread of the Presence (Leviticus 24:5–9) and the lamps lit each evening (Exodus 27:20–21). But Solomon's Temple had ten lampstands and ten tables (4:7–8; 1 Kings 7:49). The single lampstand matches the tabernacle and the Temple of the Chronicler's own day, which had one lampstand (the one later carved on the Arch of Titus). Many scholars take the detail as a sign that the speech reflects Second Temple practice. Others suggest one main lampstand was used daily.

a: trumpets of the battle blast
p: Moses' law told Israel to sound the trumpets in war so that God would remember them.
b: "When you go out to battle in your own land against an enemy who is attacking you, sound the battle blast on the trumpets. Then the LORD your God will remember you" (Numbers 10:9). Abijah's priests do exactly that (13:14). The scene follows the pattern of Jericho, where priests with horns went ahead of the army (Joshua 6:4–20). Chronicles turns the battle into a liturgy: the decisive weapons are prayer, the priests' trumpets and the war cry.

a: Israelites, don't make war on the LORD
p: Abijah's speech is one of the great set speeches of Chronicles. It speaks to all Israel, not just Judah.
b: Gerhard von Rad called speeches like this "Levitical sermons": they cite Scripture, warn and invite. Abijah's speech sums up the Chronicler's view of the split. The LORD gave the kingdom to David's house for all time (13:5); the north rebelled and drove out the true priests (13:6–9); Judah has kept the Temple worship (13:10–11). Yet he still calls the northerners "Israelites" and appeals to "the God of your ancestors." Many scholars hear the Chronicler's own hope for the people of the old northern territories in his day: the door back to Jerusalem is open (compare 30:6–9). Critical scholars doubt that a ninth-century speech was preserved word for word; traditional readers take it as the substance of what Abijah said.

a: because they had leaned on the LORD
p: The verb "lean" (sha'an) runs through these chapters: Judah leans on the LORD, Asa later leans on Aram.
b: The Niphal of sha'an means to lean or rely on something for support. Judah wins because it leaned on the LORD (13:18). Asa prays, "we lean on you" (14:11). Later Hanani the seer condemns him: "Because you leaned on the king of Aram and did not lean on the LORD your God" (16:7–8). Isaiah uses the same verb for leaning on Egypt instead of the Holy One of Israel (Isaiah 10:20; Isaiah 31:1). The word turns Asa's story into a lesson about trust.

a: Bethel and its villages
p: Bethel, home of Jeroboam's calf shrine, falls to Judah. Kings says nothing about it.
b: Bethel lay about ten miles north of Jerusalem, just across the border, and it was one of Jeroboam's two royal shrines (1 Kings 12:29). Its capture would have been a stinging blow. Kings does not mention it, and by the time of Amos, Bethel is Israel's "king's sanctuary" again (Amos 7:13). Judah may have held it only briefly. Jeshanah is probably Burj el-Isaneh, a few miles north of Bethel. On Ephrain, see the variant.

a: The LORD struck him, and he died.
p: By Kings' dates, Jeroboam outlived Abijah by a year or two.
b: Asa became king in Jeroboam's twentieth year, and Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years (1 Kings 15:9; 1 Kings 14:20). So Jeroboam did not die during Abijah's three-year reign. Chronicles probably joins the two events by theme rather than time: Jeroboam never recovered from this defeat, and his death came as the LORD's blow. Kings tells how his son died and his dynasty ended (1 Kings 14:1–18; 1 Kings 15:25–30). Some rabbinic readers took "him" to be Abijah, whom they thought God punished for the slaughter; most interpreters take it to mean Jeroboam.

a: commentary of the prophet Iddo
p: The Hebrew word here is midrash. In Chronicles it means a written study or account, not the later rabbinic genre.
b: Midrash comes from darash, "seek, study," the key verb of Chronicles. It appears in the Bible only here and in 24:27 ("the commentary on the scroll of the kings"). Later, "midrash" became the name of rabbinic interpretation of Scripture, but here it probably means a written work, perhaps one that expanded or explained older records. Chronicles has already cited Iddo's writings for Solomon and Rehoboam (9:29; 12:15). Traditional readers take these as real prophetic records. Many critical scholars think the Chronicler's citations name prophets associated with each reign, while the main source was Kings itself; some think he had other written sources as well.

a: In his days the land was quiet for ten years.
p: In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 13:23, so every verse of chapter 14 there is one number lower than in English Bibles.
b: English Bibles follow the Latin Vulgate's chapter break, which starts Asa's reign at 14:1. Hebrew printed Bibles end chapter 13 with Abijah's burial, so English 14:2 is Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:15 is Hebrew 14:14. This site uses the English numbers. The note about ten quiet years begins a pattern in Asa's story: years of quiet and rest (14:5–6; 15:15, 19) come with seeking the LORD, and wars come when he stops (16:9).

a: to seek the LORD
p: Darash, "seek," is the verb Chronicles uses for a whole life turned toward God.
b: Darash means to seek, ask, inquire or care for. In Chronicles it describes the right relationship with God: the good king "seeks the LORD," the bad one "does not seek" him (1 Chronicles 10:13–14; 2 Chronicles 12:14). These chapters use it again and again: Asa's command (14:4), Azariah's promise (15:2), the covenant (15:12–13), Asa's failure (16:12), Jehoshaphat's faith (17:3–4; 19:3; 20:3) and the burial of Ahaziah, "Jehoshaphat's son, and Jehoshaphat sought the LORD with all his heart" (22:9). It is not one ritual act but a direction of life. The promise behind it is Moses': "you will find him, when you seek him with all your heart and with all your being" (Deuteronomy 4:29).
r: Deuteronomy 4:29; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14; 1 Chronicles 28:9; 2 Chronicles 7:14; 2 Chronicles 15:2; 2 Chronicles 15:12–13

a: incense altars
p: The Hebrew hammanim has been read as "images," "sun pillars" and "incense altars."
b: The KJV has "images" here, and older scholars linked the word to chammah, "sun," giving "sun pillars." Inscriptions from Palmyra and elsewhere use a related word, chmn', for a small altar, and small stone altars for burning incense have been found across Israel and its neighbors. So most modern versions read "incense altars." The word appears with high places in Moses' warning (Leviticus 26:30) and in the prophets (Isaiah 17:8; Ezekiel 6:4–6).

a: large shields and spears
p: Judah's troops carry the big body shield; Benjamin's are archers with small shields.
b: The tsinnah was a large shield covering most of the body, used with a thrusting spear in close formation. The magen was a small round shield, carried by archers and light troops. Benjamin was known for its archers and slingers (Judges 20:16; 1 Chronicles 8:40; 1 Chronicles 12:2). On the size of the numbers, see 13:3.

a: Zerah the Cushite
p: Cush was the land south of Egypt, on the upper Nile. Zerah's identity is one of the puzzles of Chronicles.
b: Kushi usually means someone from Cush, the region of Nubia (modern Sudan), which the Greek calls Ethiopia. Three main views exist. An Egyptian army: Zerah was a Nubian commander serving a pharaoh of the Twenty-second Dynasty, perhaps Osorkon I, Shishak's son, following up Shishak's raid (12:2–9); Hanani's mention of Cushites and Libyans (16:8), the troops of Shishak's army (12:3), supports this (Kitchen). A desert people: others point to the plunder of tents, sheep and camels around Gerar (14:14–15) and think of "Cushites" living in the Negev or Arabia (compare "Cushan," Habakkuk 3:7), perhaps settled there by Shishak. A theological tale: some critics doubt any historical core. No Egyptian record names Zerah.

a: a thousand thousands
p: Literally "a thousand thousands," a million. It may be meant as "a countless army."
b: The phrase elef alafim, "a thousand thousands," is a million. Chronicles uses the same phrase for David's silver, "a thousand thousand talents" (1 Chronicles 22:14), and David's census counts 1,100,000 men in Israel (1 Chronicles 21:5). The Greek renders it word for word, "thousand thousands" (checked in Rahlfs). Daniel's Aramaic has a similar phrase for the countless servants around God's throne (Daniel 7:10). Here it may be a way to say "beyond counting," set against three hundred chariots, a realistic figure. On large numbers in Chronicles, see 13:3.

a: for you there is no difference in helping, whether the side is great or has no strength
p: Literally "there is none with you to help between great and no strength." The phrase can be read several ways.
b: The Hebrew is compressed. Most take it to mean that it makes no difference to God whether he helps the strong or the weak (KJV "it is nothing with thee to help"). Others read it as "there is no one like you to help the weak against the strong." Either way the thought matches Jonathan's: "The LORD is not held back. He can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6). Asa's prayer is the first of three great battle prayers in 2 Chronicles (14:11; 20:6–12; 32:20). Each one admits weakness and appeals to God's name.

a: Gerar
p: A town in the western Negev, between Gaza and Beersheba, known from the stories of Abraham and Isaac.
b: Gerar is probably Tel Haror, about fifteen miles northwest of Beersheba. Abraham and Isaac lived there as guests of Abimelech (Genesis 20; Genesis 26). The area was grazing land, which fits the herds, tents and camels that Judah carried off (14:14–15).

a: the dread of the LORD was on them
p: Pachad YHWH is a God-sent panic that falls on enemies.
b: In the stories of the patriarchs and the conquest, a "terror of God" falls on the towns around Israel so that they do not attack (Genesis 35:5; Exodus 15:16; Joshua 2:9). Chronicles uses "the dread of the LORD" here, in Jehoshaphat's peaceful years (17:10) and in his charge to the judges (19:7), and "the dread of God" after the victory at Beracah (20:29). It is a mark of the LORD's war, where God, not the army, wins.
r: Genesis 35:5; Exodus 15:16; Joshua 2:9; 2 Chronicles 17:10; 2 Chronicles 19:7; 2 Chronicles 20:29

a: Azariah son of Oded
p: A prophet known only from this chapter. Chronicles often gives a prophet a speech at a turning point.
b: Chronicles names many prophets that Kings does not: Azariah, Hanani (16:7), Jahaziel (20:14), Eliezer (20:37) and Zechariah son of Jehoiada (24:20). Others, such as Shemaiah (12:5) and Jehu son of Hanani (19:2), Kings names but tells little of. The phrase "the Spirit of God was on him" marks a prophet's inspiration, as with Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18). Critical scholars note that these speeches share the Chronicler's own vocabulary and often quote earlier prophets; traditional readers see the prophets as the source of the history (see 20:34).

a: Seek him, and he will let you find him.
t: "Seek him and he will be found"
p: Azariah's promise echoes Moses and Jeremiah: those who seek God find him.
b: The verb is a reflexive form of "find": God lets himself be found, or lets people find him. Moses promised that even in exile Israel would find the LORD "when you seek him with all your heart and with all your being" (Deuteronomy 4:29). Jeremiah wrote to the exiles, "You will look for me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13), and Isaiah urged, "Look for the LORD while he lets himself be found" (Isaiah 55:6). David's charge to Solomon has the same two sides, in the same Hebrew words: "Seek him, and he will let you find him. Leave him, and he will cast you aside forever" (1 Chronicles 28:9). It is close to a summary of the whole book.

a: For many days Israel had no God of truth, no priest who taught, and no law.
p: The Hebrew has no verb, so the verse can be past, present or future.
b: Literally, "Many days for Israel without a God of truth, without a teaching priest, without law." Most translations take it as past history, and many readers think of the chaos of the judges (Judges 17:6; Judges 21:25). Others hear a description of the northern kingdom since Jeroboam, which had expelled the true priests (13:9). Some ancient and medieval readers, and some modern ones, take it as prophecy, like Hosea's "For many days the Israelites will stay with no king and no prince" (Hosea 3:4–5), pointing to exile. All three readings make the same point: when Israel turned back in distress, God was found (15:4).

a: there was no peace for anyone going out or coming in
p: Azariah's description of chaos uses the words of the prophet Zechariah.
b: Zechariah described the days before the Second Temple was rebuilt: "there was no peace for the one going out or coming in, because of the enemy" (Zechariah 8:10). The next verse here (15:6) and the promise "your work will have its reward" (15:7, from Jeremiah 31:16) also borrow prophetic words. Many scholars see the Chronicler weaving later prophecy into his prophets' speeches, so that Asa's story speaks to readers in the Persian period.

a: the towns he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim
p: Kings mentions no conquests by Asa in Ephraim. These may be the towns Abijah took (13:19).
b: Chronicles may be referring loosely to the border towns Abijah captured (13:19), or to gains from Asa's own border war with Baasha (16:1–6). 17:2 also mentions "the Ephraim towns his father Asa had taken." Kings speaks only of constant war between Asa and Baasha (1 Kings 15:16). The towns explain why northerners came over to Asa (15:9).

a: Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon
p: People from the northern tribes move south to Judah. Chronicles keeps "all Israel" in view.
b: Chronicles twice reports northerners coming over to Judah because the LORD was there: priests and Levites under Rehoboam (11:13–17), and these settlers under Asa. Simeon's territory lay inside Judah in the far south (Joshua 19:1–9), so its mention among northern groups is surprising. Some think Simeonites had moved north, others that Chronicles simply means all the tribes outside Judah and Benjamin. The theme returns at Hezekiah's Passover (30:11, 18) and Josiah's reform (34:9).

a: in the third month
t: A covenant at the Feast of Weeks?
p: The third month was the time of the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot. Later Jewish tradition linked it to the covenant at Sinai.
b: The Feast of Weeks fell fifty days after Passover, in the third month (Leviticus 23:15–16). Israel arrived at Sinai "in the third month" (Exodus 19:1). The Book of Jubilees (second century BC) makes the Feast of Weeks the festival of covenant renewal, and later Judaism made Shavuot the celebration of the giving of the law. Many scholars think Chronicles hints at this: in Hebrew, "oath" (shevu'ah, 15:14–15) sounds like "weeks" (shavu'ot). Whether the Chronicler intended the wordplay is debated.

a: Whoever did not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death
t: A covenant with a death penalty
p: The oath carries the death penalty for anyone who will not seek the LORD. How should readers take it?
b: The clause applies the laws of Deuteronomy, which demand death for those who lead Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6–10; Deuteronomy 17:2–7), to the whole covenant community. Some commentators read it as an actual law enforced under Asa. Others think it is the language of a covenant oath, a curse the swearers call down on themselves if they break faith, rather than a record of executions. Jewish tradition later limited such penalties so strictly that they were almost never carried out. Christian readers have usually read it in light of Jesus' rejection of force in matters of faith (Luke 9:54–55). The phrase "from the least to the greatest" shows no one, king or commoner, man or woman, was exempt.

a: he took away the rank of queen mother from her
p: This verse is copied from 1 Kings 15:13, with one added verb: Asa "crushed" the image.
b: Chronicles follows Kings almost word for word here, and the Plain uses Kings' English (see the notes on 1 Kings 15:13 for the rank of queen mother and the rare word "horrid thing"). It adds that Asa crushed the image before burning it, as Moses ground the golden calf to powder (Exodus 32:20) and as Josiah crushed the Asherah (2 Kings 23:6). On Maacah as Asa's "mother," see 13:2.

a: The high places were not taken away from Israel
t: Did Asa remove the high places or not?
p: 14:3–5 say Asa removed the high places; this verse says he did not. Jehoshaphat's story has the same tension.
b: Kings says only that Asa left the high places (1 Kings 15:14). Chronicles says both that he removed them (14:3, 5) and that he did not (15:17), and makes the same double statement about Jehoshaphat (17:6; 20:33). Interpreters suggest: two kinds of shrine: Asa removed high places of foreign gods but not local shrines to the LORD; two regions: "from Israel" means the northern towns he controlled (15:8), not Judah; two periods: early zeal, later slackness; two sources: the Chronicler kept Kings' line beside his own report. Medieval Jewish commentators took the first or second line, and most modern ones combine them.

a: There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign.
p: Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year, by Kings' dates. How could he attack Judah in Asa's thirty-sixth (16:1)?
b: Kings says Baasha became king in Asa's third year and reigned twenty-four years (1 Kings 15:33; 1 Kings 16:8), so he was dead by Asa's twenty-sixth year. Three kinds of answer are given. Counted from the division: the rabbinic chronology Seder Olam, followed by Rashi and by Edwin Thiele, reads "the thirty-sixth year of the kingdom" as counted from the split under Rehoboam, which would be Asa's sixteenth year. A copying error: many scholars think the numbers were once fifteen and sixteen (compare 15:10) or twenty-five and twenty-six, and were changed when the letters used as numerals were misread. The Chronicler's own scheme: others think Chronicles shapes Asa's forty-one years into a faithful period of peace followed by a late fall, and is not working from Kings' figures. The Greek has the thirty-fifth here but the thirty-eighth in 16:1 (see the variant).

a: Asa brought out silver and gold
t: What Chronicles changes in Kings' account
p: Most of 16:1–6 is copied from Kings. The changes, and the new scene that follows, turn a clever move into a sin.
b: In 1 Kings 15:16–22 the treaty with Ben-hadad is told without comment, and it works: Baasha stops building Ramah. Chronicles copies the account closely but drops Kings' word "payment" (shochad, the usual word for a bribe) and the note that Asa took "all" that was left in the treasuries. Then it adds Hanani's rebuke (16:7–10), which judges the treaty as a failure of faith. Kings' remark that "War went on between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days" (1 Kings 15:16) becomes, in Chronicles, a punishment: "From now on there will be wars for you" (16:9). Where the Hebrew of the two books is the same, the Plain uses the same English, so these differences show.

a: Abel-maim, and all the store towns of Naphtali
p: Kings has "Abel-beth-maacah, and all Kinnereth." Chronicles has "Abel-maim" and "store towns."
b: Abel-maim ("meadow of waters") is another name for Abel-beth-maacah, the town at the northern tip of Israel near Dan (Tel Abil el-Qameh). The difference between Kings' "all Kinnereth" (the region of the Sea of Galilee) and Chronicles' "all the store towns" is harder. The Hebrew words share several letters (kinnerot, miskenot), and many scholars think one book's text was damaged in copying. Either way, Ben-hadad seized Israel's northern frontier, opening a long series of wars between Aram and Israel.

a: Hanani the seer
p: Hanani is known only from Chronicles. His son Jehu prophesies to Baasha and later to Jehoshaphat.
b: Hanani is called ro'eh, "seer," the old word for a prophet (1 Samuel 9:9). His son Jehu condemned Baasha in Kings (1 Kings 16:1–7) and confronts Jehoshaphat in Chronicles (19:2), and his writings are cited as a source (20:34). Hanani is the first prophet in Chronicles to suffer for his message (16:10). On "seer" and "visionary," see 19:2.

a: that is why the king of Aram's army got away from you
p: Asa never fought Aram. In what sense did Aram's army "get away"?
b: The rebuke is puzzling, because Asa bought Aram as an ally. Readers suggest: a missed victory: had Asa trusted God, he would have defeated both Baasha and his ally Aram, as he defeated Zerah's larger army (16:8); a future enemy: the Aramean army he strengthened would later invade Judah (24:23–24); a text problem: a few scholars read "the army of the king of Israel," which fits the story better, though no manuscript of Chronicles has it (the Greek also has Aram). The first reading fits Hanani's point about trust.

a: the LORD's eyes roam all over the earth
p: Hanani borrows a line from the prophet Zechariah.
b: In Zechariah's vision, the seven lamps are "the eyes of the LORD, which roam over the whole earth" (Zechariah 4:10). The Hebrew of Chronicles is nearly identical. The image is of God's watchful care, looking for those who are wholehearted, so that he can act for them. Proverbs speaks of the LORD's eyes in the same way: "In every place the LORD has his eyes open, / on the lookout over evil people and good" (Proverbs 15:3).

a: You have acted like a fool in this.
p: The prophet's words to Asa are Samuel's words to Saul.
b: The verb sakhal, "act foolishly," is what Samuel said to Saul when he offered the sacrifice instead of waiting: "You have acted like a fool" (1 Samuel 13:13). David uses it of himself after the census (1 Chronicles 21:8). Asa, the reforming king, now stands where Saul stood: a king who relied on his own plans instead of the LORD.

a: put him in the prison with the stocks
p: Mahpekhet, "the twister," was a device for locking a prisoner in a painful position.
b: The word comes from haphak, "to turn, twist." The same device held Jeremiah (Jeremiah 20:2–3), and a priest in Jeremiah's time was told to put "every madman who acts the prophet" into it (Jeremiah 29:26). Asa is the first king in Chronicles to persecute a prophet; Joash will go further and kill one (24:21). In the same breath, Asa "crushed" some of his own people, the word used for oppressing the poor (1 Samuel 12:3–4; Amos 4:1).

a: only the healers
t: Was it wrong to see doctors?
p: Asa is blamed for seeking "healers" instead of the LORD. Does the Bible condemn medicine?
b: The Hebrew rophe'im means "healers" or "physicians." Not medicine but trust: most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, think the fault was seeking doctors instead of God, not seeking doctors at all; Ben Sira later praises physicians but tells the sick to pray first (Ben Sira 38:1–15). The Talmud reads Exodus 21:19, "sees that he is fully healed," as God's permission for doctors to heal (Bava Kamma 85a). Pagan healers: some think the healers were magicians or priests of other gods (compare 2 Kings 1:2–3). A wordplay: some scholars note that with different vowels the word could be repha'im, the spirits of the dead. The LORD had called himself "your healer" (Exodus 15:26), and Asa's story ends with the same word that ran through it: he did not seek.
r: Exodus 15:26; Exodus 21:19; 2 Kings 1:2–3; Ben Sira 38:1–15; Jeremiah 8:22

a: his sickness rose higher and higher
p: Literally "until upward his sickness." It may mean the illness spread up his body or grew very severe.
b: Kings says only that "when he grew old he got a sickness in his feet" (1 Kings 15:23); see the note there on gout, gangrene and other guesses. Chronicles adds a date, two years before his death, and the phrase ad lema'lah, "up to above," which elsewhere means "exceedingly" (26:8). Either sense fits: the disease climbed or it grew extreme.

a: Then they lit a great fire for him, very great.
p: This was not a cremation. Israel burned spices and other things in honor of a dead king.
b: Israel buried its dead and did not burn bodies. The fire was a burning of spices and perhaps of the king's belongings, a mark of honor. Jeremiah promised Zedekiah, "As burnings were made for your fathers... so people will make a burning for you" (Jeremiah 34:5). The Talmud regards burning a king's bed and belongings at his death as a lawful Israelite custom (Avodah Zarah 11a). Jehoram is denied this honor (21:19). Kings says only that Asa "was buried with his ancestors in the city of his forefather David" (1 Kings 15:24). Chronicles replaces this with a tomb Asa had cut for himself, a bier full of spices and the fire: a deliberate picture of honor for a king it has just criticized. Chronicles' verdict on a king often shows in how he was buried (21:20; 24:16, 25; 26:23).
r: 1 Kings 15:24; Jeremiah 34:5; 2 Chronicles 21:19–20; 2 Chronicles 24:16; 2 Chronicles 24:25; 2 Chronicles 26:23

a: he made himself strong against Israel
t: Strong against Israel, then allied with it
p: Jehoshaphat begins by fortifying his border against the north. Later he marries his son into Ahab's family.
b: Kings gives Jehoshaphat ten verses (1 Kings 22:41–50) and mentions him in Ahab's and Jehoram's wars (1 Kings 22; 2 Kings 3). Chronicles gives him four chapters (17–20). The reign has a clear shape: strength and reform (17), the alliance with Ahab and a rebuke (18:1–19:3), judicial reform (19:4–11), a great deliverance (20:1–30), and a second failed alliance (20:35–37). The first move, guarding the border with Israel, contrasts with the later marriage alliance (18:1). Kings simply reports, "Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel" (1 Kings 22:44).

a: the ways his forefather David had walked at first
t: David's first ways, or his father's?
p: The Hebrew says "the first ways of David his father." The Greek lacks "David," making it Asa's early ways.
b: "His father" in Hebrew can mean any forefather, and Jehoshaphat's father was Asa. With "David," the phrase probably means David's ways in contrast to the later kings, or David's early years, before the census and other failures. Without "David," as in the Greek (see the variant), it means Asa's good early years, before his treaty with Aram and his illness (16:1–12). That reading fits Chronicles' portrait of Asa well, which is why some scholars think "David" was added by a scribe who expected the usual formula.
orig: בְּדַרְכֵי דָּוִיד אָבִיו הָרִאשֹׁנִים (bedarkhe David aviv harishonim)

a: His heart rose high in the LORD's ways.
p: "His heart was high" usually means pride. Here it means courage or zeal for the LORD.
b: Gavah lev, "the heart was high," is normally a bad sign: Uzziah's and Hezekiah's hearts grew proud (26:16; 32:25), and "a high heart" is hateful to the LORD (Proverbs 16:5). Here alone it is used in a good sense, "in the LORD's ways": Jehoshaphat was bold and eager for God. Some versions translate "courageous," others "devoted." The same phrase thus describes both the virtue and the vice that grows out of it.

a: to teach in Judah's towns
p: Officials, Levites and priests tour Judah teaching the law. Is this ninth-century history or a picture of Ezra's day?
b: Chronicles alone reports this mission. Traditional readers accept it as history; the king's name, Jehoshaphat, "the LORD judges," fits his reforms of teaching and justice (19:4–11). Many critical scholars think the scene reflects the Chronicler's own time, when Levites taught the law to the people (Nehemiah 8:7–9; compare Deuteronomy 33:10), and was set in Jehoshaphat's reign because of his name. Others, such as W. F. Albright and Gary Knoppers, think it rests on a real royal reform, retold in later language. The mix of royal officials, Levites and priests is unusual and may be an old detail.

a: the scroll of the LORD's law
p: Chronicles says the teachers carried "the scroll of the LORD's law." What book did they have?
b: The phrase can mean the whole Torah, the five books of Moses, as it does in Chronicles' own day (34:14; Nehemiah 8:1–3). Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take it that way. Critical scholars who date Deuteronomy or the Pentateuch later than Jehoshaphat think the Chronicler is describing the law as he knew it, or that an earlier law code is meant. The scene anticipates Josiah, who found "the scroll of the LORD's law" in the Temple (34:14) and read it to the people.

a: The Arabs also brought him flocks
t: Tribute from the Philistines and the Arabs
p: Jehoshaphat receives tribute from neighbors on two sides, a sign of God's blessing in Chronicles.
b: Tribute from foreign peoples marks a king blessed by God in Chronicles, as with Solomon (9:23–24) and Uzziah (26:8). "Arabs" here means desert peoples of the Negev and northern Arabia, whose wealth was in flocks and camels. Arab tribes appear first in the Bible's histories in Chronicles (17:11; 21:16; 22:1; 26:7) and in Assyrian records of the same period, which mention Arab camel troops at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC.

a: This is how they were enrolled by their families.
t: An army of over a million
p: The five commanders lead 1,160,000 men, besides the town garrisons.
b: The totals in 17:14–18 add to 1,160,000, close to the 1,100,000 that David's census counted for Israel alone (1 Chronicles 21:5; Judah's 470,000 came on top). Readers handle the size as with Abijah's armies (see 13:3): as literal, as units counted in elef groups, or as the Chronicler's way of showing God's blessing on a faithful king. The commanders' names may come from an old muster list.

a: who offered himself freely to the LORD
p: Amasiah "made himself a free offering" to the LORD, perhaps as a volunteer for holy war.
b: The verb hitnaddev is used for freewill gifts to the Temple (1 Chronicles 29:5–9; Ezra 1:6) and for warriors who volunteered in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:2, 9). Some think Amasiah took a vow, perhaps like a Nazirite (Numbers 6), others that he simply enlisted without being called up.

a: he tied himself to Ahab by marriage
p: Jehoshaphat married his son Jehoram to Ahab's daughter Athaliah. Chronicles calls it the root of later disasters.
b: The verb hitchatten means to become related by marriage. The marriage of Jehoram of Judah to Athaliah (21:6; 22:2) sealed peace between the two kingdoms after decades of war. Chronicles judges it harshly: through Athaliah the house of Ahab nearly wiped out David's line (22:10). Kings uses the related noun chatan, "son-in-law," of Ahaziah's tie to Ahab's house (2 Kings 8:27). Placing the marriage right after "riches and honor" may hint that Jehoshaphat's success made him a desirable partner, or made him overconfident.

a: he coaxed him into going up against Ramoth-gilead
p: Ahab "lured" Jehoshaphat into the war; in 18:31 God "lured" the attackers away from him. The same verb is used.
b: Hesit means to entice or incite, often to something wrong (Deuteronomy 13:6; 1 Chronicles 21:1). Chronicles uses it twice in this chapter as a frame. Ahab coaxes Jehoshaphat into the battle (18:2); God coaxes the enemy chariots away from him (18:31). Between them stands Micaiah's vision, where a spirit offers to "lure" Ahab (a different verb, pitta, 18:19–21, kept as in 1 Kings 22). The Plain uses "coax" for hesit and "lure" for pitta so the two verbs stay apart. Chronicles adds both uses of hesit; neither is in Kings.

a: I am one with you, my people one with your people
p: Jehoshaphat uses the same words to Ahab here and to Ahab's son Jehoram in the Moab war.
b: In 1 Kings 22:4 the formula ends "my horses one with your horses." Chronicles ends instead "we will be with you in the battle." Jehoshaphat says it again to Jehoram of Israel: "I am one with you, my people one with your people, my horses one with your horses" (2 Kings 3:7). The phrase is the language of a full alliance. Jehu son of Hanani will condemn exactly this (19:2).

a: But Jehoshaphat also told the king of Israel
t: Why Chronicles tells this northern story
p: Chronicles leaves out almost all of the northern kingdom's history, but copies 1 Kings 22 nearly word for word.
b: Chronicles does not tell the stories of Elijah, Elisha, Ahab or Jezebel. It keeps Micaiah's story because Judah's king is in it. From 18:4 to 18:34 the Hebrew follows 1 Kings 22:5–35 closely, so the Plain uses the site's wording of 1 Kings 22 wherever the words match. The differences are small but telling: "God" for "the Lord" (18:5), "all his days" (18:7), Micaiah's answer without the LORD's name (18:14), and above all the LORD's help for Jehoshaphat (18:31). Chronicles leaves out the dogs licking Ahab's blood and the fulfillment of Elijah's word (1 Kings 22:36–40). For the deeper questions of the chapter, the heavenly council and the lying spirit, see the notes on 1 Kings 22.

a: God will hand it over to the king.
p: Kings has the court prophets say "the Lord" (Adonai). Chronicles has "God" (ha-Elohim).
b: The change is small but typical. Chronicles often uses "God" where its source has the LORD's name or "Lord." In Kings, some readers see a hint that the four hundred speak of a vague "Lord" rather than the LORD (see the note on 1 Kings 22:6). In Chronicles the hint is gone, or changed: they speak of "God" in general, while Jehoshaphat asks for "a prophet of the LORD" (18:6).

a: They will be handed over to you.
p: In Kings Micaiah says, "The LORD will hand it over to the king." In Chronicles he does not use the LORD's name.
b: Chronicles' Micaiah answers with the plural "Go up and win" and "They will be handed over to you," without naming the LORD. Many readers think this sharpens the sarcasm: Micaiah echoes the court prophets' tone but will not attach the LORD's name to a false promise (compare his oath in 18:13). The king hears at once that he does not mean it (18:15).

a: Micah
p: Here the Hebrew calls the prophet by the short form "Micah"; Kings has "Micaiah" in the same verse.
b: Everywhere else in this chapter the prophet is Mikhayehu, "Micaiah," "Who is like the LORD?" In the king's question the Hebrew of Chronicles has the short form Mikhah, "Micah," while 1 Kings 22:15 keeps Micaiah. It is the same man; short and long forms of names often alternate (Joash and Jehoash, Joram and Jehoram). The Plain follows each verse's Hebrew, so the change is visible.

a: I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets
p: Chronicles keeps the scene of the LORD sending a lying spirit, though elsewhere it changes the LORD's role in evil.
b: Where 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD incited David to take a census, Chronicles says "Satan" or "an adversary" did (1 Chronicles 21:1). Many scholars see this as Chronicles shielding God from causing sin. Yet here it copies the lying spirit unchanged. Some explain that the lying spirit brings judgment on Ahab, who is already condemned, rather than leading the innocent into sin. Others note that Chronicles had no reason to alter a scene it treats as a prophet's vision. For the main views on how God could send a lying spirit, see the note on 1 Kings 22:22 and the topic on the evil spirit from the LORD.

a: Joash, the king's son
p: This may be one of Ahab's sons, or an official title for a royal officer.
b: No son of Ahab named Joash is known. In several places "the king's son" seems to be the title of an officer with police duties: Jerahmeel "the king's son" was sent to arrest Jeremiah, and Jeremiah was thrown into the cistern of Malchiah "the king's son" (Jeremiah 36:26; Jeremiah 38:6). Seals with the title "son of the king" have been found. Either reading fits Micaiah being handed to the city's jailers.

a: The LORD came to his aid; God coaxed them away from him.
p: Kings says only that Jehoshaphat cried out. Chronicles adds that the LORD heard and drew the attackers away.
b: The Chronicler turns Jehoshaphat's cry into a prayer and its result into a rescue. Kings leaves open what the cry was, a battle cry or a cry of panic that showed he was not Ahab (see the note on 1 Kings 22:32). Chronicles answers: it was a cry to the LORD, and God "coaxed" the chariot commanders away. The addition sets up the prophet's rebuke in 19:2: God saved the king even in a war he should never have joined.

a: he died at the time the sun went down
p: Chronicles ends the story at Ahab's death. It leaves out the blood in the chariot, the dogs and the burial.
b: In 1 Kings 22:35–38 the blood pools in the chariot, the army scatters, and dogs lick up Ahab's blood at the pool of Samaria, as Elijah had said (1 Kings 21:19). Chronicles never told Elijah's word against Ahab, so it does not tell its fulfillment either. It also never names Ahab after 18:19. The northern king dies at sunset, and the story turns at once to Jehoshaphat's safe return (19:1). Chronicles also has "the king of Israel" where Kings has "the king," "until evening" where Kings speaks of his dying "in the evening," and an active verb, "held himself up," where Kings has "was kept standing up."

a: came back in peace
p: Ahab vowed to come back "in peace" and did not (18:26–27). Jehoshaphat, the one he put in danger, does.
b: Micaiah had said, "If you really do come back in peace, the LORD has not spoken through me" (18:27). Chronicles has already sharpened the echo: where Kings has Ahab say bo'i, "my coming," Chronicles has shuvi, "my return," the same verb Micaiah uses in his reply (18:26–27); the Plain says "come back" in both verses. The narrator now uses the same word, beshalom, of Jehoshaphat. His safe return is the proof of Micaiah's word from the other side, and the setting for the prophet who meets him at the gate.

a: Jehu son of Hanani the visionary
p: Hanani was "the seer" (ro'eh, 16:7). His son Jehu is "the visionary" (chozeh).
b: Hebrew has several words for a prophet: navi, "prophet"; ro'eh, "seer," the older word (1 Samuel 9:9); and chozeh, "visionary" or "one who sees visions." Chronicles uses all three (1 Chronicles 29:29). This site keeps them distinct: "seer" for ro'eh, "visionary" for chozeh. Jehu son of Hanani already prophesied against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1, 7), some forty years earlier.

a: Is it those who hate the LORD you should love?
t: Loving those who hate the LORD
p: Jehu condemns the alliance with Ahab as "loving those who hate the LORD." What kind of love is meant?
b: In ancient treaties, "love" was the word for political loyalty between allies, and "hate" for hostility; William Moran showed that Deuteronomy's command to "love" God draws on this language. So Jehu's charge is not about personal feelings but about alliance: Jehoshaphat has pledged loyalty to a king the LORD opposes. Interpreters apply the verse differently. Some Jewish and Christian readers take it as a warning against binding alliances with the wicked (compare 2 Corinthians 6:14); others stress that Jehu at once adds "good things have been found in you" (19:3), and that Jesus taught love for enemies (Matthew 5:44), so the point is not personal hatred but whose side one takes.

a: made your heart ready to seek God
p: Hekhin lev, "to set or prepare the heart," is a favorite Chronicles phrase for steady devotion.
b: Of Rehoboam it says, "He had not made his heart ready to seek the LORD" (12:14). Jehoshaphat did (19:3), though the people still had not (20:33). Hezekiah prays for "everyone whose heart is set on seeking God" (30:19). The same Hebrew phrase describes Ezra, who "had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law, to doing it, and to teaching" (Ezra 7:10), perhaps a hint of the Chronicler's ideal.

a: from Beersheba to Ephraim's hill country
p: The old phrase for all Israel was "from Dan to Beersheba." For Judah it is from Beersheba to the northern hills.
b: Beersheba marked the southern edge of settled land; the hill country of Ephraim began just north of Jerusalem, where Asa held towns (15:8; 17:2). The king himself goes out among the people, like the teachers in 17:7–9, turning them back to the LORD. Chronicles uses "from Beersheba to Dan" for Hezekiah's call to all Israel (30:5).

a: He set judges in the land
p: Jehoshaphat ("the LORD judges") sets up local and central courts. Is this an old reform or a later picture?
b: The reform closely follows Deuteronomy: judges in every town (Deuteronomy 16:18–20) and a central court of priests and a judge in the chosen place (Deuteronomy 17:8–13). Some scholars, starting with W. F. Albright, argued that Jehoshaphat really organized Judah's courts and that Deuteronomy's laws later reflect such a system. Others think the Chronicler built the scene from Deuteronomy and the king's name, picturing the courts of his own day. Many take a middle view: a memory of a ninth-century reform, told in later terms. The sermon to the judges (19:6–7, 9–10) is in any case one of the Bible's clearest statements of justice as service to God.

a: It is not for people that you judge, but for the LORD.
p: Jehoshaphat's charge echoes Moses: "the judgment is God's."
b: Moses told Israel's first judges, "Do not be afraid of anyone, because the judgment is God's" (Deuteronomy 1:17). The judge stands in God's place, so God is present "in the matter of judgment." The next verse continues with Deuteronomy's description of God: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Psalm 82 pictures God judging the judges who fail.

a: between one kind of bloodshed and another
p: The phrase means deciding between different kinds of killing, such as murder and accidental death.
b: Deuteronomy uses the same words for hard cases sent to the central court: "one kind of bloodshed or another, one claim or another" (Deuteronomy 17:8). The law distinguished deliberate murder from accidental killing (Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 19:1–13). The central court in Jerusalem was to teach and warn the local judges ("your brothers") so that wrong verdicts would not bring guilt on the whole people.

a: in every matter of the LORD
t: The LORD's matters and the king's
p: Jerusalem's court has two heads: a priest for religious cases, a royal officer for the king's.
b: Amariah the head priest handles "every matter of the LORD," Zebadiah "every matter of the king." The division of religious and civil authority resembles the Persian period, when the high priest and the governor shared leadership (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 4:14), and Ezra was charged with enforcing "your God's law and the king's law" (Ezra 7:26). Some scholars take this as a sign of the Chronicler's own setting, others as an old arrangement. Some later readers saw an early form of the distinction between religious and civil courts. The Levites serve as shoterim, officials who kept records and passed on orders.

a: from beyond the Sea
p: The enemy comes from the east side of the Dead Sea and is already at En-gedi on its western shore.
b: "The Sea" is the Dead Sea. The coalition of Moab, Ammon and Mount Seir (Edom's hill country) came around its southern end and up the western shore to En-gedi, a spring and oasis halfway along the coast, also called Hazazon-tamar ("Hazazon of the palms," Genesis 14:7). From there a steep path climbs to Tekoa and Bethlehem, only a day's march from Jerusalem. On "Aram" or "Edom," see the variant.
r: Genesis 14:7; 1 Samuel 24:1; Song of Songs 1:14; Ezekiel 47:10

a: He called for a fast throughout Judah.
p: The first national fast in Chronicles. Fasting and prayer replace troop counts.
b: Unlike Abijah and Asa, Jehoshaphat assembles no army list here. He calls a fast, and Judah gathers at the Temple to seek the LORD. National fasts were called in crises (Judges 20:26; 1 Samuel 7:6; Joel 1:14; Joel 2:15; Jonah 3:5; Ezra 8:21–23). The scene acts out Solomon's prayer: when war comes, the people will pray toward this house, and God will hear (6:34–35; 7:13–14).

a: in front of the new courtyard
p: Which courtyard was "new" is unknown.
b: Solomon built an inner "courtyard of the priests" and a "great courtyard" (4:9). The "new" courtyard may be one of these renewed by Asa, who repaired the altar before the porch (15:8), or an addition later than Solomon. Some scholars think the Chronicler had the outer court of the Second Temple in mind.

a: the offspring of your friend Abraham
p: Abraham is called God's friend here, in Isaiah and in James. In Arabic tradition he is "the Friend of God."
b: The Hebrew ohavkha is literally "the one who loves you." God says through Isaiah, "offspring of Abraham, who loved me" (Isaiah 41:8). James writes that Abraham believed God "and he was called God's friend" (James 2:23). In Islam Abraham's title is Khalil Allah, "God's friend" (Qur'an 4:125), and Hebron, his burial place, is called al-Khalil. Jehoshaphat appeals to the promise of the land to Abraham's offspring "for all time" (Genesis 13:15).

a: we will take our stand before this house
p: Jehoshaphat holds God to the promise made when the Temple was dedicated.
b: The list "sword, judgment, plague or famine" and the promise to stand before the house and cry out sum up Solomon's dedication prayer (6:20–40) and God's answer (7:12–16). Jehoshaphat stands in the same courtyard and prays as Solomon taught: in trouble, look to this house, where God's name dwells. His prayer has the classic shape of a lament: praise of God's power (20:6), memory of his past acts (20:7–9), the present danger (20:10–11), and a plea of trust (20:12).

a: you did not let them go into these lands
p: God had forbidden Israel to attack Ammon, Moab and Edom on the way from Egypt. Now these nations attack.
b: Moses was told, "Do not harass Moab, and do not stir them up to war" (Deuteronomy 2:9), and the same for Edom (Deuteronomy 2:4–5) and Ammon (Deuteronomy 2:19), since these lands were given to Esau and Lot. Israel went around them (Numbers 20:14–21; Judges 11:15–18). Jehoshaphat's argument is that Israel kept the LORD's command and spared them, and now they repay that mercy by trying to drive Israel out of the LORD's own property.

a: Our eyes are on you.
p: The king's prayer ends not with a plan but with a confession of helplessness.
b: The psalms use the same picture: "I keep my eyes turned to the LORD at all times" (Psalm 25:15), "See how slaves keep their eyes on their master's hand ... That is how our eyes are on the LORD our God" (Psalm 123:2), and "my eyes are on you, LORD, my Lord" (Psalm 141:8). The admission "What we should do, we do not know" sets up the answer from the Levite prophet (20:14–17).

a: one of Asaph's sons
p: The answer comes through Jahaziel, a Levite of Asaph's guild of singers.
b: Chronicles says David set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, who "prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 25:1–3). Here a descendant of Asaph speaks a prophetic oracle. Many scholars think this reflects the Chronicler's own time, when the Levitical singers' psalms and words were honored as inspired. Traditional readers see Jahaziel as one more of the prophets God raised up at the right moment. His five-generation pedigree, unusual for a prophet, underlines his Levitical standing.

a: The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God.
p: Jahaziel's words recall David before Goliath and Moses at the Sea.
b: David told Goliath, "The battle belongs to the LORD, and he will put you in our power" (1 Samuel 17:47). The command "Don't be afraid, and don't panic" is the standard opening of a war oracle (Deuteronomy 1:21; Deuteronomy 31:8; Joshua 8:1). In the LORD's war, Deuteronomy says, "the LORD your God is the one who goes with you, to fight for you" (Deuteronomy 20:4).

a: the Ascent of Ziz
p: The enemies were climbing the pass from the Dead Sea toward Tekoa.
b: The Ascent of Ziz is usually identified with the route up the Wadi Hasasa, north of En-gedi, which climbs to the plateau near Tekoa. The "wilderness of Jeruel" is unknown, but must lie in the dry country between Tekoa and the Dead Sea. Tekoa, the home of Amos, stood on the edge of this wilderness (Amos 1:1).

a: Take your stand, stand still, and watch the LORD save you
p: Jahaziel repeats Moses' words at the Sea of Reeds.
b: With the Egyptians behind them, Moses told Israel, "Do not be afraid. Take your stand, and see how the LORD will save you today" and "The LORD will fight for you" (Exodus 14:13–14). The Hebrew verbs here are the same: take your stand, see the LORD's salvation. Judah's victory is a new exodus in which the people only watch. In both stories the next scene is singing (Exodus 15:1; 2 Chronicles 20:21–28).

a: Hold firm to the LORD your God, and you will be held firm.
p: Jehoshaphat's words play on one Hebrew root, aman, "firm," the root of "believe" and "amen."
b: Ha'aminu, "believe, hold firm," and te'amenu, "you will be made firm, be established," come from the same root. Isaiah used the same play to King Ahaz: "If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm" (Isaiah 7:9). Jehoshaphat turns Isaiah's warning into a promise, and adds "hold firm to his prophets," trust in the word just given through Jahaziel. Faith here is not a feeling but leaning one's weight on what God has said, the opposite of Asa's leaning on Aram (16:7).

a: to praise in holy splendor
p: Hadrat qodesh can mean the splendor of God's holiness, or the holy attire of the worshipers.
b: The phrase appears in the psalms: "bow down to the LORD in the splendor of holiness" (Psalm 29:2; Psalm 96:9; 1 Chronicles 16:29). The KJV has "the beauty of holiness." Some take hadrah to mean adornment or clothing, so the singers wore holy robes (compare 1 Chronicles 15:27). Others take it as the majesty of God himself. A Ugaritic parallel suggests a meaning "appearance, vision," so some translate "when he appears in holiness." The Plain keeps the Hebrew's bare "to praise in holy splendor," which leaves both senses open.

a: Give thanks to the LORD, for his loyal love is forever.
p: The singers use the refrain that rang out when the ark came to Jerusalem and the Temple was dedicated.
b: The line is the Temple's great refrain (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3, 6; Ezra 3:11), repeated after every line of Psalm 136. Chesed, "loyal love," is God's faithfulness to his covenant. The army's front line is a choir singing about God's love, not about the enemy.
r: 1 Chronicles 16:34; 1 Chronicles 16:41; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 2 Chronicles 7:3; Psalm 136:1; Ezra 3:11

a: the LORD put men in ambush
p: The text does not say who the "ambushers" were. The enemies then destroy each other.
b: Readers have suggested: heavenly agents, angels sent against the enemy (many Jewish and Christian interpreters); human raiders, perhaps local men or a group within the enemy camp; or confusion that made the allies think they were ambushed by one another. What follows is clear: Ammon and Moab turn on Mount Seir, then on each other. The same thing happened in Gideon's battle, when "the LORD turned each man's sword against his comrade all through the camp" (Judges 7:22), and in Jonathan's (1 Samuel 14:20). Ezekiel pictures God's final victory the same way (Ezekiel 38:21).

a: to put them under the ban
p: The enemies apply the "ban," total destruction, to their own allies.
b: Haḥarim, "to devote to destruction," is the verb of the ban, the total destruction of an enemy given over to God in holy war (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21). Here the irony is sharp: Judah never fights, and the enemies carry out the ban on each other.

a: the Valley of Beracah
p: Beracah means "blessing." The name survives near Tekoa.
b: The valley is named for the thanksgiving held there: "there they blessed (berakhu) the LORD." The name may survive at Khirbet Bereikut and the Wadi Bereikut, a few miles west of Tekoa, on the road between Bethlehem and Hebron. As often in the Bible, a place-name preserves the memory of an event "to this day."

a: The people still had not made their hearts ready
p: Kings says the people still sacrificed at the high places. Chronicles says their hearts were not ready.
b: 1 Kings 22:43 says, "The people still offered sacrifices and burned offerings at the high places." Chronicles replaces this with a judgment on the heart, using its favorite phrase (see 19:3). It also leaves the failure with the people, not the king, who had removed high places (17:6). On the double statement about high places, see 15:17.

a: the words of Jehu son of Hanani
p: Chronicles cites a work by Jehu the prophet, "taken up into the scroll of the kings of Israel."
b: Where Kings refers readers to "the day-by-day records of the kings of Judah" (1 Kings 22:45), Chronicles names a prophet's writing that was included in a larger royal history. For Chronicles, prophets were the historians of the kings (1 Chronicles 29:29; 2 Chronicles 9:29; 2 Chronicles 32:32). Jewish tradition called Joshua through Kings "the Former Prophets" for the same reason. Chronicles calls Judah's history "the kings of Israel," because it sees Judah as the true Israel. Whether these works existed separately or are the Chronicler's names for parts of Kings is debated (see 13:22).

a: He did wickedly in doing so.
p: The Hebrew can mean Ahaziah "acted wickedly," or that Jehoshaphat did wrong by joining him.
b: Literally, "he acted wickedly to do." Many translations make Ahaziah the subject: "Ahaziah king of Israel, who acted wickedly" (compare 1 Kings 22:52). Others make Jehoshaphat the subject: he did wrong in making the deal, which fits Eliezer's rebuke (20:37). The Plain keeps the Hebrew's ambiguity.

a: to sail to Tarshish
p: Kings: "Tarshish ships" for Ophir, and Ahaziah's help refused. Chronicles: ships "to go to Tarshish," built together.
b: Ezion-geber lay on the Gulf of Aqaba, on the Red Sea, the port for Ophir (1 Kings 9:26–28). Tarshish was far to the west, on the Mediterranean, probably in Spain or Sardinia. In Kings, "Tarshish ships" means large ocean-going ships (see the note on 1 Kings 22:48). Chronicles speaks of ships "to go to Tarshish," which many scholars think misreads the phrase, though some think of a voyage around Africa. Kings says Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's offer to send sailors (1 Kings 22:49); Chronicles says they were partners from the start. Harmonizers suggest the refusal came after the wreck. Most critical scholars think the Chronicler reshaped Kings to make the disaster a judgment on the alliance.

a: Eliezer son of Dodavahu, from Mareshah
p: A prophet known only from this verse, from the town where Asa beat Zerah (14:9–10).
b: His father's name, Dodavahu, means "beloved of the LORD." Mareshah lay in the Shephelah, the foothills west of Hebron. Eliezer's one-line oracle follows the pattern of Chronicles: an act, a prophet's verdict, and a swift result. The ships' wreck becomes the fulfillment of his word.

a: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariahu
p: The list has Azariah and Azariahu, two forms of the same name, for two different brothers.
b: Azaryah and Azaryahu are short and long forms of one name, "the LORD has helped." Two sons with the same name would be odd. Some scholars think one name was miscopied from another (the Syriac has a different name for one of them); others note that half-brothers by different mothers could bear the same popular name. The list is unique to Chronicles and probably comes from a family record.

a: Then he killed all his brothers with the sword
t: Murder at the start of a reign
p: Only Chronicles reports that Jehoram killed his six brothers and some officials.
b: Killing rival heirs was a common way to secure a new king's throne in the ancient world. Abimelech killed his seventy brothers (Judges 9:5), Jehu wiped out Ahab's sons (2 Kings 10:6–7), and Athaliah will kill the royal family (22:10). The brothers had been given rich gifts and fortified towns (21:3), which made them possible rivals. Elijah's letter names this crime (21:13), and Jehoram's punishment mirrors it: his own sons are carried off (21:17). The "officials of Israel" probably means leaders of Judah, whom Chronicles often calls Israel.

a: because of the covenant he had made with David
p: Kings: the LORD would not destroy Judah. Chronicles: he would not destroy David's house, because of his covenant.
b: 2 Kings 8:19 reads, "because of his servant David, the LORD did not want to wipe out Judah." Chronicles changes "Judah" to "David's house" and "his servant David" to "the covenant he had made with David." The focus moves from the land to the dynasty, which fits what follows: the house of David is about to come within one baby of extinction (22:10–12). The "lamp" is a living heir on the throne (see the note on 2 Kings 8:19).

a: Jehoram went across with his commanders
p: Kings ends this battle with "the people fled to their tents." Chronicles omits that line.
b: In Hebrew, Kings' place name "to Zair" (tsa'irah) and Chronicles' "with his commanders" (im sarav) look alike, and one is probably a misreading of the other (see the variant at 2 Kings 8:21). Chronicles also drops Kings' last words, "the people fled to their tents," which suggest a rout. The result reads like an escape by night rather than a defeat. Yet Chronicles adds its own reason for the revolts: Jehoram "had left the LORD" (21:10).

a: He led the people of Jerusalem into prostitution
p: The verb zanah, "to prostitute oneself," is the prophets' image for worshiping other gods.
b: Israel's covenant with the LORD was pictured as a marriage, so worshiping other gods was adultery or prostitution (Exodus 34:15–16; Hosea 1:2; Jeremiah 3:1–9; Ezekiel 16). Chronicles uses the verb only here, in Elijah's letter (21:13), and of the northern tribes long before (1 Chronicles 5:25). It probably refers to Baal worship brought in with Athaliah (compare 24:7).

a: a writing came to him from Elijah the prophet
p: Elijah appears in Chronicles only in a letter, yet Kings seems to place his going up before Jehoram's reign.
b: 2 Kings 2 tells of Elijah's ascension, and 2 Kings 3:11 then has Elisha serving in Jehoshaphat's lifetime as the one "who poured water over Elijah's hands." So how could Elijah write to Jehoram? Still alive: Josephus says Elijah was still on earth. Kings itself dates the end of Ahaziah of Israel, while Elijah was active, to "the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat" (2 Kings 1:17), suggesting Jehoram ruled alongside his father, and Kings does not tell its stories in strict order. Written in advance or sent from heaven: the rabbinic chronology Seder Olam places the letter after Elijah was taken up, and medieval Jewish commentators explained it as written beforehand by prophecy or delivered after his departure. A literary device: many critical scholars think the Chronicler composed it in Elijah's name, as the great prophet against Ahab's house; its language is the Chronicler's own.

a: until day after day your bowels come out from the disease
p: What illness is meant is unknown. The Bible and later writers tell similar deaths of wicked rulers.
b: Modern guesses include chronic dysentery, a prolapse of the bowel and colon cancer. The illness lasts two years (21:19). The detail belongs to a pattern in ancient writing, where tyrants die of loathsome diseases of the gut: Antiochus IV in 2 Maccabees 9:5–9, Herod the Great in Josephus, Herod Agrippa, "eaten by worms" (Acts 12:23), and Judas, whose "insides spilled out" (Acts 1:18). Elijah's sentence matches the crime: a king who destroyed his own flesh and blood is destroyed from within.

a: the Arabs who were next to the Cushites
p: Philistines from the west and Arab tribes from the south raid Judah. The Cushites are probably those of 14:9.
b: Under Jehoshaphat these same Philistines and Arabs had paid tribute (17:11). Now they invade. The "Cushites" next to the Arabs are probably not Nubians far up the Nile but a people living in the Negev or western Arabia, like Zerah's (see 14:9). Kings mentions none of this; it records the revolts of Edom and Libnah (2 Kings 8:20–22).

a: Jehoahaz
p: The youngest son is called Jehoahaz here and Ahaziah in 22:1. Both names mean "the LORD has taken hold."
b: Yeho'achaz and Achazyahu are made of the same two parts, "the LORD" and "has grasped," in reverse order. Chronicles uses both forms for the same king, and the Greek has "Ahaziah" here (Ochozias). On this site, each name is kept in the form its verse uses, with a note when two forms name one person. A later king of Judah, Josiah's son, is also called Jehoahaz (36:1).

a: He passed on with no one missing him.
p: Kings says Jehoram was buried with his ancestors. Chronicles says he was buried, unmourned, outside the royal tombs.
b: Literally "he went without desire," that is, no one wanted him back. 2 Kings 8:24 says, "Joram lay down with his ancestors and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David." Chronicles keeps the City of David but takes away the royal tombs and the honor-fire (21:19). The same verdict is passed on Joash (24:25), on leprous Uzziah (26:23) and on Ahaz (28:27), while the priest Jehoiada is buried among the kings (24:16). Harmonizers note that "with his ancestors" in Kings can mean simply "in death." Jeremiah's word against Jehoiakim is similar: no one will lament him (Jeremiah 22:18–19).
r: 2 Kings 8:24; 2 Chronicles 24:16; 2 Chronicles 24:25; 2 Chronicles 26:23; 2 Chronicles 28:27; Jeremiah 22:18–19

a: the war band that had come into the camp with the Arabs
p: The raiders of 21:16–17 had killed Jehoram's older sons. Kings knows nothing of this.
b: Chronicles explains why the youngest son became king, and why the people of Jerusalem had to make him king. In Kings, Ahaziah simply succeeds his father (2 Kings 8:24). The pattern of the whole story is grim: Jehoram killed his brothers (21:4); raiders kill his sons; Jehu kills Ahaziah's nephews (22:8); Athaliah kills the rest (22:10). Only one baby survives.

a: for his mother advised him to act wickedly
p: Kings blames Ahaziah's marriage ties to Ahab's house. Chronicles blames his mother and her family as his advisers.
b: 2 Kings 8:27 explains Ahaziah's sins by his ties to Ahab's house. Chronicles puts it in terms of counsel: his mother was his adviser, and after his father's death Ahab's family became his advisers "to his ruin." The word "counsel" runs through 22:3–5, as it ran through Rehoboam's bad choice of advisers (10:6–14). Some modern readers suggest that a young king surrounded by his mother's relatives was hardly free to choose.

a: and the Arameans wounded Joram
p: Within one verse, Ahab's son is called both Jehoram and Joram. The Hebrew uses both forms.
b: Yehoram and Yoram are long and short forms of one name, "the LORD is exalted." In these years both kingdoms had a king of that name: Jehoram of Judah, Jehoshaphat's son, and Jehoram or Joram of Israel, Ahab's son, who were brothers-in-law. The Hebrew of both Kings and Chronicles switches between the forms for each king. This site keeps the form each verse uses rather than making them uniform (the same policy is followed for Joash and Jehoash). Here Chronicles also writes "the Arameans" in an unusual way (see the variant).

a: It was God's doing that Ahaziah was brought down
p: Tevusah, "downfall," is found only here. Chronicles sees God's hand in Ahaziah's fatal visit.
b: The word comes from bus, "trample," so it means a crushing defeat. Kings tells Ahaziah's death as part of Jehu's purge (2 Kings 9:27–28), without comment. Chronicles adds a theological frame: God arranged that Ahaziah would be in Jezreel when Jehu struck. The same pattern appears with Rehoboam (10:15, "from God") and Amaziah (25:20). For Chronicles, alliances with Ahab's house bring ruin.

a: the sons of Ahaziah's brothers who waited on Ahaziah
p: Kings says Jehu killed forty-two "brothers of Ahaziah." Chronicles says "the sons of Ahaziah's brothers."
b: 2 Kings 10:12–14 tells how Jehu met forty-two "brothers of Ahaziah" on the road and killed them. Since Chronicles has already said Ahaziah's brothers were killed by raiders (21:17), it speaks of their sons. "Brothers" can mean relatives in general, so the two accounts may describe the same group. The Greek here reads simply "brothers of Ahaziah." The order also differs: in Kings Jehu kills Ahaziah first and the relatives later; in Chronicles the relatives die first.

a: He was caught hiding in Samaria
p: Kings, Chronicles and an Aramean inscription give different accounts of how Ahaziah died.
b: Kings: Ahaziah fled from Jezreel, was struck near Ibleam, died at Megiddo and was buried in Jerusalem (2 Kings 9:27–28). Chronicles: he hid in Samaria, was found, brought to Jehu and executed, and "they" buried him out of respect for Jehoshaphat. The Tel Dan inscription (about 840 BC), written for an Aramean king, probably Hazael, claims "I killed [Jeho]ram son of [Ahab] king of Israel, and I killed [Ahaz]iahu son of [Jehoram] king of the house of David," though the names are partly restored. Harmonizers suggest Ahaziah hid in Samaria, was caught, wounded while escaping, and died at Megiddo; or that Hazael claimed credit for a coup he supported. Many scholars think Chronicles simply retold the event briefly in its own way. The Greek has Ahaziah caught "being treated for his wounds" in Samaria, not hiding (see the variant), which would bring Chronicles closer to Kings' wounded king.

a: And Ahaziah's house had no one left with the strength to keep the kingdom.
p: Ahaziah's sons were small children. No one in the family could take the throne.
b: Ahaziah reigned one year. His son Joash was a baby (22:11; 24:1). The verse explains how Athaliah could seize power: there was no grown male heir. In Chronicles the house of David hangs on one infant, the low point of God's promise of a lasting dynasty (13:5; 21:7).

a: destroyed
p: Chronicles uses dibber, a rare verb meaning "destroy," where Kings has "wiped out."
b: The Hebrew wattedabber is spelled like the common verb "speak," but here it comes from a rarer root meaning "subdue" or "destroy" (compare Psalm 18:47, "who brings nations down beneath me," from the same root). Kings has watte'abbed, "she wiped out" (2 Kings 11:1). The two words differ in two letters that are easily confused in Hebrew script, so one may be a copying change. The sense is the same. On Athaliah's coup, see the notes on 2 Kings 11:1.

a: wife of Jehoiada the priest
t: A princess married to a priest
p: Only Chronicles says Jehoshabeath was Jehoiada the priest's wife, which explains how the boy hid in the Temple.
b: Kings calls her Jehosheba (2 Kings 11:2); Chronicles' longer form is Jehoshabeath. Both mean "the LORD is an oath." She is the daughter of King Jehoram and sister (or half-sister) of Ahaziah, so her marriage linked the royal house and the high priestly family. Whether she was Athaliah's own daughter is not said; many think she was born to another wife. It is the only marriage between a princess and a priest that the Bible records, and it made Jehoiada the boy's uncle by marriage.

a: In the seventh year Jehoiada took heart.
p: Chronicles follows 2 Kings 11 but keeps foreign guards out of the Temple and gives the Levites the leading role.
b: In Kings, Jehoiada works with the officers of the Carites (probably foreign mercenaries) and "the runners," the royal guard, who stand inside the Temple around the king (2 Kings 11:4–11). Chronicles names five Judean officers (23:1), brings in the Levites from all Judah (23:2), and insists that only priests and Levites enter the house "because they are holy" (23:6). The Carites and runners disappear. Most scholars see the Chronicler's concern for the holiness of the Temple and the role of the Levites in his own day. Some traditional readers argue that the Levites were present all along, and Kings, written for other reasons, simply did not mention them.

a: just as the LORD said of David's sons
p: Jehoiada grounds the coup in God's promise to David.
b: The phrase recalls Nathan's oracle, that God would raise up David's offspring and set up his throne for all time (1 Chronicles 17:11–14), and the promise repeated to Solomon (6:16; 7:18). Chronicles has already said that the LORD did not wipe out David's house because of his covenant (21:7). Jehoiada's words make the coup an act of loyalty to that promise, not just a palace revolt.

a: the ones who come in on the Sabbath
p: Priestly and Levite divisions changed duty on the Sabbath. Jehoiada used the change to have twice as many men on hand.
b: The priests and Levites served in divisions that rotated weekly, changing on the Sabbath (1 Chronicles 24:1–19; Luke 1:8–9). At the change, the outgoing division had not yet left and the incoming one had arrived. Jehoiada "had not let the divisions go" (23:8), so he had both shifts at once. See also the note on 2 Kings 11:5.

a: the Foundation Gate
t: Foundation Gate or Gate of Sur?
p: Kings names "the Gate of Sur." Chronicles has "the Foundation Gate."
b: In Hebrew the two names, sur and yesod, look alike, since the letters for d and r were easily confused. Neither gate is mentioned elsewhere. One book probably has a copying error, but which one is uncertain. Some take "foundation gate" as a gate at the base of the palace complex.
orig: שַׁעַר הַיְסוֹד (sha'ar hayesod); Kings שַׁעַר סוּר (sha'ar sur)

a: All the people must keep what the LORD has charged them to keep.
p: Mishmeret YHWH means the duty or watch the LORD assigns. Here it keeps the crowd outside the holy house.
b: Mishmeret means a guard post, a duty, or an obligation to be kept. The priests and Levites go into the house; "all the people" stay in the courtyards (23:5) and keep the LORD's charge, which here means obeying the rule that only the holy may enter. In Numbers the Levites "keep the charge" of the tabernacle so that outsiders do not come near and die (Numbers 1:53; Numbers 18:3–5).

a: the bucklers
p: The word rendered "bucklers" (shelatim) is rare and its sense is debated.
b: Chronicles lists three items: spears, maginnot (shields) and shelatim. Kings has "spear and shields," using shelatim for "shields" (2 Kings 11:10). The word appears only a few times (2 Samuel 8:7; Song of Songs 4:4; Jeremiah 51:11; Ezekiel 27:11). Some take it as a kind of shield, others as quivers or ceremonial weapons hung on walls. The Plain uses "bucklers" here to keep the three Hebrew words apart.
r: 2 Kings 11:10; 2 Samuel 8:7; Song of Songs 4:4; Jeremiah 51:11; Ezekiel 27:11

a: Jehoiada and his sons anointed him
p: Kings says "they" anointed him. Chronicles names Jehoiada and his sons.
b: In Kings the people clap and shout. Chronicles leaves out the clapping and makes the priests the anointers, as Zadok anointed Solomon (1 Kings 1:39). Jehoiada's sons are probably the priests who served with him, among them Zechariah (24:20). The "testimony" given to the king may have been a copy of the law or a covenant document (see the note on 2 Kings 11:12; compare Deuteronomy 17:18).

a: the singers with their instruments of song were leading the praise
p: Chronicles adds Levite singers to the coronation and reads Kings' "runners" as people "running."
b: Kings speaks of "the sound of the runners and the crowd" (2 Kings 11:13), the runners being the royal guard. Chronicles has "the people running and praising the king" (23:12), so a word that meant a guard unit becomes a description of the crowd. In 23:13 it adds the Levite singers with their instruments leading the praise. For the Chronicler, every great event of the kingdom is accompanied by the Temple's music (1 Chronicles 15:16; 2 Chronicles 5:12–13; 2 Chronicles 20:21; 2 Chronicles 29:25–30).

a: a covenant between himself and all the people and the king
t: Jehoiada as a party to the covenant
p: Kings: a covenant between the LORD, the king and the people. Chronicles: between Jehoiada, the people and the king.
b: In 2 Kings 11:17 Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD and king and people, and another between king and people. In Chronicles Jehoiada himself is a party. Some scholars think the priest acts in the LORD's place, as Moses did at Sinai. Others think the Chronicler's text read differently. Others see the Chronicler giving the high priest a greater role, as in the Persian period. The goal is the same in both: "that they would be a people belonging to the LORD."

a: as the law of Moses has it written, with joy and with song, by David's direction
p: Sacrifices are offered by Moses' law, and the singing follows David's direction. Chronicles gives both their place.
b: Chronicles often names two authorities for Temple worship: Moses for the sacrifices (Exodus; Leviticus; Numbers) and David for the music and the Levites' duties (1 Chronicles 23–26). Jehoiada restores both after Athaliah's years. The same double formula returns at Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms (29:25–30; 35:4–6, 15). Kings says only that the priest appointed overseers over the house (2 Kings 11:18). The noun is the same, pequddot; the Plain says "posts of oversight" here because Chronicles places them "in the hands of" the Levite priests, so it means the offices rather than the men.

a: the Upper Gate
p: Kings names the Runners' Gate. Chronicles has the Upper Gate and again replaces the guards with nobles and rulers.
b: Where 2 Kings 11:19 lists "the Carites, the runners" and "the Runners' Gate," Chronicles has "the nobles, the rulers of the people" and "the Upper Gate," which Jotham later rebuilt (27:3). Both changes fit Chronicles' omission of the foreign guards (see 23:1). The Upper Gate probably led from the Temple courts down to the palace (compare Jeremiah 20:2).

a: Joash
