p: Chronicles calls this king Joash throughout. 2 Kings 12 mostly calls him Jehoash.
b: Yo'ash and Yeho'ash are short and long forms of one name, perhaps "the LORD has given." Here the Hebrew even spells it in an unusually short way. 2 Kings 12 uses Jehoash at its start and Joash at its end (2 Kings 12:19–20). A northern king of the same name, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, reigned a little later (25:17). This site keeps the form each verse has, so readers can see the Hebrew's own variety.

a: all the days of Jehoiada the priest
p: Kings says Joash did right "all his days, since Jehoiada taught him." Chronicles says "all the days of Jehoiada."
b: The Hebrew of 2 Kings 12:2 can mean "all his days in which Jehoiada taught him" (see the note there). Chronicles removes the ambiguity: Joash was good while Jehoiada lived. Then it builds the reign in two halves: faithful years and the Temple repair (24:1–14), then Jehoiada's death, apostasy, the murder of Zechariah and judgment (24:15–27). The pattern of good beginnings and bad endings is common in Chronicles (Asa, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah).

a: Jehoiada took two wives for him
p: The priest arranges the king's marriages. Sons and daughters rebuild a royal family almost wiped out.
b: After Athaliah's purge, Joash was the only male of David's line left (22:10–11). Many sons and daughters were a sign of blessing in Chronicles (11:18–21; 13:21), and here they also secure the dynasty. One of the wives, Jehoaddin of Jerusalem, was Amaziah's mother (25:1). Kings does not mention the marriages.

a: Moses' tax
p: Chronicles links the Temple repair money to the half-shekel Moses collected for the tabernacle.
b: Mas'at Mosheh, "Moses' tax," refers to Exodus 30:12–16, where each person counted gives "half a shekel, by the holy place's shekel... a gift for the LORD" (Exodus 30:13), used for the service of the tent of meeting (Exodus 38:25–28). In Kings, Joash's repair money came from three sources handled by the priests (2 Kings 12:4). Chronicles ties it to the law of Moses. In Nehemiah's day the people pledged a third of a shekel a year (Nehemiah 10:32), and by Jesus' time the half-shekel was paid yearly by Jews everywhere (Matthew 17:24–27). The root nasa, "carry," appears in these chapters as "silver by the load" (17:11), loads of plunder (20:25), and massa, "oracle" or "burden," in 24:27.

a: For Athaliah's sons, sons of that wicked woman
p: Athaliah's sons are not known. The phrase may mean her followers, or the sons of Jehoram killed earlier.
b: Literally "Athaliah the wickedness, her sons broke into God's house." Athaliah's known son Ahaziah is dead, and his brothers were killed by raiders (21:17). Suggestions include: "sons" meaning her supporters or priests of Baal (like "sons of the prophets"); Jehoram's sons before their deaths, under her influence; or a damaged text, with some scholars reading "her builders." The noun "wickedness" used as a name for a woman is unusual: "Athaliah, Wickedness itself."

a: the king's scribe came with the head priest's officer
t: The collection in Kings and in Chronicles
p: Kings and Chronicles differ on who collected, where the chest stood, and what the money bought.
b: Who: in Kings, priests collect from their acquaintances and fail to repair (2 Kings 12:4–8); in Chronicles, Levites are sent to the towns and are slow (24:5). Where: Kings sets the chest beside the altar, inside (2 Kings 12:9); Chronicles sets it outside the gate (24:8), so the people do not enter the holy area. What: Kings says no vessels were made from the money (2 Kings 12:13); Chronicles says the leftover money made vessels (24:14). Harmonizers note that Kings speaks of the time of the repairs and Chronicles of what was left afterward. Most scholars see Chronicles adapting an old account to its own Temple rules. Both agree on the scribe and the priest counting the money together.

a: under their hands the mending went forward
p: The word for repair, arukhah, also means new flesh growing over a wound.
b: Arukhah is used for the healing of a wound: "your healing will spring up quickly" (Isaiah 58:8; compare Jeremiah 8:22; Jeremiah 30:17). Nehemiah uses it for the repair of Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 4:7). The Temple is pictured as a body recovering. "To its right measure" means according to its original plan (Exodus 30:32 uses the same word for the proper formula).

a: He was a hundred thirty years old at his death.
p: Jehoiada's age is greater than Moses' or Aaron's. It is the age Jacob gave Pharaoh.
b: If Jehoiada was 130 at death, he was around a hundred at the coup and older still during the repair. Some readers accept the figure; others suspect a copying error, or take it as an honorific number. Jacob told Pharaoh, "I have been a wanderer for a hundred and thirty years" (Genesis 47:9); Moses died at 120 and Aaron at 123 (Deuteronomy 34:7; Numbers 33:39). "Had his fill of days" is said of Abraham, Isaac, David and Job (Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29; 1 Chronicles 29:28; Job 42:17).
r: Genesis 47:9; Deuteronomy 34:7; Numbers 33:39; Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29; 1 Chronicles 29:28

a: They laid him in a grave among the kings in the City of David.
p: Jehoiada is buried with the kings. Joash, the king he saved, is not (24:25).
b: No other priest in the Bible is said to have been buried in the royal tombs. Chronicles gives the reason: "he had done good in Israel, for God and for God's house." The contrast is deliberate: Jehoram (21:20) and Joash (24:25) are refused that honor. Some readers see the Chronicler's high regard for the priesthood; others, his teaching that honor goes to faithfulness, not rank.

a: came and bowed down to the king
p: After Jehoiada dies, the officials bow to the king, and he listens to them. A midrash says they made him a god.
b: Bowing to a king was ordinary court custom, but here it introduces a turn to idols (24:18). A rabbinic midrash (Exodus Rabbah 8:2) says the officials told Joash that anyone who survived six years hidden in the Holy of Holies must be divine, and he accepted their worship; the commentary printed under Rashi's name on Chronicles repeats this. The text itself says only that the king listened to the officials rather than to the priest's teaching, as Rehoboam listened to the young men (10:8–14).

a: He sent prophets among them to turn them back to the LORD
p: God sends prophets and they are not heard: the pattern that ends with the exile.
b: The last chapter of Chronicles sums up Israel's history the same way: "the LORD, the God of their ancestors, sent to them by his messengers, rising early and sending," but they mocked his prophets until there was no remedy (36:15–16). Jeremiah says the same (Jeremiah 7:25–26). Jesus tells it as the parable of the tenants (Mark 12:1–9) and speaks of Jerusalem killing the prophets (Matthew 23:37).

a: God's Spirit put on Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest like clothing
p: Literally "the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah." The Spirit wears the prophet like a garment.
b: The verb lavash, "to put on clothes," is used of the Spirit only here and twice elsewhere: of Gideon ("the Spirit of the LORD put Gideon on like clothing," Judges 6:34), of Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18), and here. The picture is of God's Spirit filling and using a person, who speaks not his own words. The son of the priest becomes a prophet, standing on a height in the Temple court.

a: Why are you going against the LORD's commands? You will not succeed.
p: Zechariah repeats Moses' words to the Israelites who tried to invade Canaan against God's command.
b: When the people set out against God's word after the spies' report, Moses said, "Why are you going against the LORD's command? It will not work" (Numbers 14:41). Zechariah's Hebrew is almost the same. The next line, "You have left the LORD, so he has left you," repeats Azariah's warning to Asa (15:2) and Shemaiah's to Rehoboam (12:5).

a: in the courtyard of the LORD's house
p: Jesus spoke of the blood of Zechariah, killed "between the altar and the house." Most think he meant this man.
b: Jesus said the prophets' blood would be required "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the house" (Luke 11:51); Matthew has "Zechariah son of Berechiah" (Matthew 23:35). Zechariah son of Jehoiada: the view of most interpreters. In the Talmud's order (Bava Batra 14b) Chronicles is the last book, so the pair runs from the first murder in Scripture to the last; Uriah was killed later in time (Jeremiah 26:20–23), so the pair is canonical, not chronological. But the Aleppo and Leningrad codices put Chronicles first among the Writings, and whether the order was fixed in Jesus' day is debated, so some take the pair as proverbial. "Son of Berechiah" may come from the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1) or Isaiah's witness Zechariah son of Jeberechiah (Isaiah 8:2). Other views: the prophet himself; John the Baptist's father (Protevangelium of James); or Zechariah son of Bareis, killed by Zealots in AD 68 (Josephus).
r: Luke 11:49–51; Matthew 23:34–36; Zechariah 1:1; Genesis 4:8–10; Isaiah 8:2; Jeremiah 26:20–23

a: they pelted him with stones
p: The law stoned blasphemers outside the camp. Zechariah, God's spokesman, is stoned inside the Temple court.
b: The law says the one who cursed the LORD was to be taken "outside the camp" and stoned (Leviticus 24:14; compare Numbers 15:36). Zechariah's enemies turn the punishment for blasphemy against the man who spoke God's word, and they do it in the holy courtyard "on the king's order." Jewish tradition remembered the crime as a terrible defilement. The Talmud and midrash tell that Zechariah's blood kept seething in the Temple court for two and a half centuries, until the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan killed thousands to quiet it (Gittin 57b; Sanhedrin 96b; Lamentations Rabbah). The Jerusalem Talmud says Israel committed seven sins that day (Taanit 4:5).

a: May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out.
p: Zechariah dies asking God to "see" and "seek out" his blood. Stephen and Jesus die asking God to forgive.
b: "Seek out" is darash, the verb of seeking God that runs through Chronicles; here it means to require an account for blood, as God "requires" a life for a life (Genesis 9:5) and Abel's blood "has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Chronicles shows the answer at once: within a year Aram's army comes and Joash is killed "over the blood" of Jehoiada's son (24:23–25). Christian readers have long contrasted these words with Jesus' "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34) and Stephen's "Lord, do not count this sin against them!" (Acts 7:60). Hebrews says Jesus' blood "speaks better" than Abel's (Hebrews 12:24). In Luke, "this generation will be called to account for it" (Luke 11:51) uses the Greek word for the same idea (ekzēteō, "seek out, require").
r: Genesis 4:10; Genesis 9:5; Luke 11:50–51; Luke 23:34; Acts 7:60; Hebrews 12:24

a: When the year came around, Aram's army marched up against him.
p: Kings says Hazael threatened Jerusalem and Joash bought him off. Chronicles tells a defeat in battle as judgment.
b: 2 Kings 12:17–18: Hazael took Gath and turned toward Jerusalem; Jehoash sent him all the holy gifts and the gold of the treasuries, and Hazael withdrew. Chronicles tells of a small Aramean army that defeated Judah's great one, killed "all the people's officials" (the same men who led the king astray, 24:17), and sent plunder to Damascus. It is the reverse of Abijah's and Asa's victories over huge armies (13:3; 14:9). The two accounts may describe different stages of one war. Chronicles' interest is the meaning: the forsaking of the LORD (24:20) brings the punishment Zechariah asked God to see.

a: Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman, and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabite woman
p: Kings names the killers' parents Shimeath and Shomer. Chronicles makes both mothers, an Ammonite and a Moabite.
b: In Kings, Shimeath and Shomer could be fathers or mothers; Chronicles takes both as women and names their peoples, Ammon and Moab. Shomer becomes Shimrith. Some scholars think the Chronicler wanted the murderers of a Davidic king to have foreign blood; others note that Ammon and Moab were the nations Deuteronomy barred from the LORD's assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), or that the names came from a fuller source. The first name also differs: Zabad here, Jozabad (or Jozacar) in Kings.

a: the great oracle against him
p: Massa can mean a burden, a tax or a prophetic oracle. Here it may be the prophets' oracles against Joash.
b: The phrase is hard. The written Hebrew (Ketiv) reads "and the greatness of the burden (massa) on him," singular; the read form (Qere) gives "may the burden on him be great." Massa is the usual title of a prophet's oracle ("The oracle concerning Babylon," Isaiah 13:1), so many take it of the prophecies against Joash (24:19–20), and translations often make it plural. The Plain follows the written form and keeps the singular, "the great oracle." Others take it as the heavy tax for the Temple (the related mas'at in 24:6, 9), or the burden of judgment on him. The Greek reads differently again. The "commentary on the scroll of the kings" uses the word midrash (see 13:22).
